## La Charca de Suárez: a unique wetland on the Granada coast

Spanning fourteen and a half hectares, the Charca de Suárez unfolds just a few meters from the coastline, on terrain where the fresh water descending from Sierra Nevada meets the saline intrusion of the Mediterranean. That mixture of flows, far from being a drawback, defines the character of the wetland and explains the biological richness it harbors. The water surface is not uniform: it alternates between dense reedbed areas, muddy shores, and small islets that emerge depending on the time of year. Each of those microhabitats serves a different function for the fauna that depends on the site.

The bird census exceeds two hundred species, a figure that places this space among the most productive on the Andalusian coast in terms of ornithological biodiversity. Among them, the marbled teal stands out, a diving duck classified as critically endangered in Spain, which finds here one of its scarce breeding refuges in the southern Iberian Peninsula. The white-headed duck, another threatened anatid, also uses the pond as a breeding and resting site. The simultaneous presence of both species turns the wetland into a natural laboratory for the technicians who monitor their populations.

The geographic location of the site is decisive for understanding its ecological role. Situated at the eastern end of the Granada coast, it functions as a service station for migratory birds crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or skirting the Mediterranean on their journeys between Europe and Africa. The ringers and ornithologists working in the area have recorded more than ten thousand specimens per year, a figure that fluctuates depending on the meteorological conditions of each migratory season. During postnuptial passages, when birds return south after breeding, the pond fills with waders, herons, and passerines that need to replenish their strength before facing the crossing.

The brackish water, that hybrid between continental and marine inputs, favors the emergence of plant communities that have learned to coexist with salinity. Tamarisks and reeds dominate the perimeter; on the more exposed shores, however, halophytic plants grow that are rarely observed elsewhere in the province. That vegetation cover not only adorns the landscape: it provides shelter and food for a trophic chain that includes amphibians, reptiles, small mammals, and a notable variety of aquatic invertebrates. The pond, in short, is not a simple spectacle for ornithology enthusiasts; it is a complete ecosystem sustained by delicate balances.

The proximity to the sea introduces an uncommon variable in the inland wetlands of Andalusia. Tides and easterly storms can alter the salinity of the lagoons within hours, and species must adapt to abrupt changes. That dynamic, which elsewhere would be a stress factor, has here become a distinctive feature. The site's managers have learned to read those natural pulses and to intervene as little as possible so as not to break the cycles that regulate the wetland's life.

The ornithological value of the site goes beyond threatened species. During winter, flocks of mallards, northern shovelers, and common pochards occupy the water surface; in spring, purple herons and little bitterns breed among the reeds. The observation hides installed around the perimeter allow visitors to contemplate these scenes without disturbing the animals, an advantage that has made the Charca de Suárez a regular destination for nature photographers and birdwatching enthusiasts from all over Spain.

The declaration as a Special Protection Area for Birds, still in process, would provide legal backing for what the biological data already demonstrate. The wetland comfortably meets the criteria established by the European Birds Directive, both in terms of the number of species present and the relevance of its breeding populations. That protection status, combined with the municipal management maintained in recent years, would safeguard the future of a space that has survived decades of neglect and urban pressure.

The Charca de Suárez is not a conventional urban park. Access is regulated, routes follow boardwalks and marked paths, and silence is part of the experience. Those who visit it for the first time are often surprised to discover that a site of these characteristics lies just minutes from the center of Motril, surrounded by greenhouses and housing developments. That condition of a natural island in a territory profoundly transformed by intensive agriculture adds supplementary value: the pond demonstrates that biodiversity can survive if given a chance.
